subject: Anthropology
title: Phonology
description: A short lesson to help you apply Phonology.

hook.text: In English, R and L are different sounds. In Japanese, they're the same. Your language trains your ears.

buildup.text: Phonology is the study of sound systems — the meaningful sound units (phonemes) that a language uses.

discovery.text: Every language selects from a limited set of possible human sounds. No language uses them all.

twist.text: Babies hear all sounds at birth. By twelve months, they've tuned in to their native language and tuned out the rest.

climax.text: Phonology shows that even hearing is cultural. Your language literally shapes what sounds you can perceive.

punchline.text: You hear what your language taught you to hear.

quiz.question: What is a phoneme?
options: A meaningful sound unit in a language

details.summary: Phonology studies the sound systems of languages — which sounds are used, how they combine, and which distinctions carry meaning. Each language selects a subset from hundreds of possible human speech sounds and organizes them into a unique system.
details.whyItMatters: Phonological systems shape how people perceive speech. Adults struggle to hear sound distinctions not used in their native language, showing how language literally shapes auditory perception from early childhood.
takeaways: Languages select different sound subsets from hundreds of possibilities
Phonemes are the smallest units that distinguish meaning in a language
Native language phonology shapes how speakers perceive all speech

faq.question: Why can't some speakers hear certain sound distinctions?
faq.answer: Infants can distinguish all human speech sounds, but by twelve months, they begin losing sensitivity to sounds not used in their native language. Japanese speakers struggle with English R/L because Japanese uses a single phoneme where English uses two.

faq.question: How many phonemes do languages typically have?
faq.answer: Languages range from about 11 phonemes (Rotokas of Papua New Guinea) to over 100 (some Khoisan languages with click consonants). English has roughly 44 phonemes. The number does not correlate with language complexity or expressiveness.
